Nolan Ashford

life-047 · holdout · fictional age 16

Written life first, then interpreted by a separate response author without the engine or results. These are synthetic checks. There is no correct career answer key.

Life from age 4 to 16

I know I've had a lot of chances, which makes saying I don't know feel embarrassing. Cooking is one thing where I can tell that I actually did something instead of just showing up where someone sent me.

  • family: Only child living with married parents; family routines are warm and quiet, and a longtime housekeeper is also a trusted adult.
  • finances: High income and substantial education savings; most practical needs are handled by adults.
  • geography: A gated development near The Woodlands, Texas.
  • cultureLanguages: White, English-speaking family; relatives gather for boating trips and birthdays, with little formal religious practice.
  • school: Small private school where most classmates expect to attend four-year universities.
  • accessOpportunities: Numerous programs are affordable, but transportation is arranged for him and he has limited experience choosing or maintaining commitments himself.
  • Age 4–5

    Nolan liked lining up toy trains and asking adults to ride the imaginary routes. He was slow to join preschool games but became animated once another child agreed to a familiar story about delivering cakes.

  • Age 6–7

    He tried tennis, chess lessons, and swimming in succession. Adults handled registration and gear, so stopping felt as simple as saying he was bored; he rarely saw how beginners became skilled through repetition.

  • Age 8–9

    A long visit with a cousin included building a rough tree platform. Nolan enjoyed fetching boards and testing where to place them, but afterward told friends mostly about the cousin’s dog rather than the construction.

  • Age 10–11

    Remote school left him spending many afternoons on video games with classmates. He liked managing shared resources in a cooperative game and quietly kept the group supplied while louder friends decided where to explore.

  • Age 12–13

    His parents encouraged a robotics camp, but he disliked the rushed team assignments and did not ask for another. An art elective interested him briefly because he could work at his own pace without a public scoreboard.

  • Age 14–15

    When the housekeeper took leave, Nolan learned laundry and several dinners. He felt unexpectedly proud when a meal came together on time, though he initially treated planning ingredients as someone else’s separate task.

  • Age 16

    He now cooks once a week and plays cooperative games with friends. College visits blur together, and he cannot yet describe a subject he wants to pursue; a patient teacher has suggested trying one ordinary commitment long enough to encounter difficulty.

Life now

  • enjoys: Cooperative games · Cooking a complete meal · Quiet company
  • avoids: Rushed team contests · Being asked for a polished future plan
  • activities: Weekly dinner · Gaming with friends · Art elective
  • demonstratedSkills: Tracks shared supplies · Follows recipes · Notices when teammates lack materials
  • unfamiliarActivities: Paid work · Public transit · Long projects with consequences
  • motivations: Feeling useful through his own effort · Maintaining friendships
  • ambitions: Unsure what comes after expected college attendance · Imagines a comfortable independent home but has little sense yet of its daily demands.
  • struggles: Low persistence when choices feel interchangeable · Few self-directed experiences
  • supports: Parents · Housekeeper · Art teacher · Friends
  • practicalConstraints: Transportation dependence · Adults often solve practical problems before he tries

Still uncertain: Would a real audience sustain his effort? · How much independence would reveal interests currently hidden by adult arrangements?
